power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Illumination and the Emergence of Creative Ideas: A Dual-Route Model

text.text: Illumination has occupied a central position in theories of creativity since Wallas identified it as one of the four phases of the creative process.

Although subsequent models have continued to recognize illumination as the moment at which new ideas emerge into awareness, relatively little attention has been devoted to the cognitive processes underlying this transition.

At the same time, a parallel literature on insight problem solving has generated extensive evidence describing the processes that precede and accompany the sudden emergence of new ideas, yet these findings have rarely been integrated into broader theories of creativity.
This chapter brings together these traditions to reconsider illumination within the broader process of creative idea generation.
Building on classical and contemporary theories of creativity, a Dual-Route Model of Creative Idea Generation is proposed.
In the continuous route, intermediate states remain accessible to conscious awareness as an idea develops.
By contrast, in the discontinuous route, an idea becomes abruptly available to conscious awareness, following processing that is not fully accessible to introspection.

Behavioral, metacognitive, and neurocognitive evidence relevant to these different modes of idea emergence is reviewed, alongside their potential relationships with the quality and subsequent memory of the ideas generated.

Finally, the broader implications of the framework are considered by examining insight as a possible form of model updating, outlining the main empirical predictions of the Dual-Route Model, and discussing its relevance to creative problem solving in engineering and design.
How do creative ideas come to mind?
This apparently simple question has occupied philosophers, scientists, artists, and psychologists for centuries.
Creative work does not always unfold in the same way.
Some ideas develop gradually through deliberate reasoning; others emerge suddenly, with little conscious awareness of how they were reached.
An engineer might design a new device by progressively modifying its components, testing alternatives, and improving the design step-by-step.

In other cases, a solution may arise from suddenly seeing the problem differently, for example, realizing that an assumed constraint is unnecessary or that a component could serve an entirely different function.
Both outcomes can be creative, but the experience of reaching them differs.

The first experience feels like building an idea progressively; the second, like discovering one. Kuhn (1962) argued that scientific revolutions are driven by discontinuous shifts that give rise to new paradigms, rather than by continuous, cumulative progress within an existing conceptual framework.
text.formatted: The first experience feels like building an idea progressively; the second, like discovering one. <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Kuhn (1962)</ref> argued that scientific revolutions are driven by discontinuous shifts that give rise to new paradigms, rather than by continuous, cumulative progress within an existing conceptual framework.

text.text: New paradigms enable researchers to ask new theoretical questions of existing data, moving beyond the "puzzle-solving" of the former paradigm and changing the framework that directs subsequent research.
While Kuhn explained scientific progress rather than individual cognition, his account offers a useful parallel for understanding how creative ideas emerge.

Some creative ideas develop gradually, much like the cumulative progress of science within an established paradigm; others emerge when the existing conceptual framework shifts abruptly, opening up new questions, interpretations, and solutions to problems.
Just as a scientific revolution changes the perspective from which existing knowledge is understood, an insight can suddenly reveal a new way of looking at a familiar problem.

Research on insight problem solving offers an experimental literature for investigating how ideas emerge through these two routes and, in particular, the illumination phase described in theories of creative cognition. Wallas (1926) distinguished four stages of creativity: preparation, incubation, illumination, and verification.
text.formatted: Research on insight problem solving offers an experimental literature for investigating how ideas emerge through these two routes and, in particular, the illumination phase described in theories of creative cognition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Wallas (1926)</ref> distinguished four stages of creativity: preparation, incubation, illumination, and verification.

text.text: Preparation involves acquiring relevant knowledge and beginning work on the problem.
Incubation refers to an interval during which deliberate work is suspended, allowing for the possibility of continued processing outside awareness.
Illumination marks the appearance of the "happy idea," often described as a "flash" of understanding, and verification involves evaluating, refining, and developing the idea toward implementation.
Long before modern cognitive psychology, several scholars tried to describe the illumination phase in similar terms.

At the end of the nineteenth century, Hermann von Helmholtz, the physicist and physiologist, described how, after investigating a problem thoroughly, "happy ideas come unexpectedly without effort, like an inspiration" (Helmholtz, as quoted in Wallas, 1926, p. 80; Wallas cites Rignano, 1923, pp. 267-268).

text.text: Others noted that such ideas often arise during a peaceful walk or periods of rest (Ochse, 1990; Wallas, 1926). Einstein and Infeld (1938, p. 4) illustrated the sudden emergence of an idea through Conan Doyle's detective stories: after gathering seemingly unrelated clues, an investigator turns away from the problem.

text.text: In Einstein and Infeld's account, "[...] plays his violin, or lounges in his armchair enjoying a pipe, when suddenly, by Jove, he has it!"
These descriptions capture the phenomenology of illumination remarkably well, but not all creative ideas are characterized by such sudden emergence.
Several subsequent theories elaborated and refined different aspects of Wallas's original framework.

Earlier discussions encompassed diverse approaches, including those of Epstein (1990); Milgram (1990), alongside accounts of insight, invention, and creative transformation (Feldman, 1988; Langley and Jones, 1988; Ohlsson, 1984; Perkins, 1988; Simonton, 1988). Campbell (1960) proposed an evolutionary account of creative thought based on blind variation and selective retention.
text.formatted: Earlier discussions encompassed diverse approaches, including those of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Epstein (1990)</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Milgram (1990)</ref>, alongside accounts of insight, invention, and creative transformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Feldman, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Langley and Jones, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Ohlsson, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Perkins, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Simonton, 1988)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Campbell (1960)</ref> proposed an evolutionary account of creative thought based on blind variation and selective retention.

text.text: This framework distinguishes the production of alternatives, the selection of successful variants, and the retention of selected outcomes.
Building on this approach, Simonton (1988) developed a chance-configuration account in which creativity arises through permutations of mental elements.
text.formatted: Building on this approach, <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Simonton (1988)</ref> developed a chance-configuration account in which creativity arises through permutations of mental elements.

text.text: These elements constitute the basic units available for combination and recombination during the creative process.
Through such combinatorial processes, novel configurations may arise, leading to a creative idea.
The appearance of such a configuration is not, however, the end of the creative process.
The individual must engage in conscious work to transform it into a communication configuration: a symbolic form through which the insight can be expressed and made available to others.
Simonton's account therefore distinguishes the emergence of an idea from the deliberate work required to articulate and develop it.

Building on the broader distinction between the generation and subsequent selection or development of creative possibilities, Finke et al. (1992) advanced the Geneplore model, which provided a more explicit cognitive account of recurring generative and exploratory activity.
text.formatted: Building on the broader distinction between the generation and subsequent selection or development of creative possibilities, <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Finke et al. (1992)</ref> advanced the Geneplore model, which provided a more explicit cognitive account of recurring generative and exploratory activity.

text.text: Generative processes concern the construction of loosely formulated ideas called preinventive structures and include knowledge retrieval, association, synthesis, transformation, and analogical transfer.
These structures are preliminary possibilities rather than fully specified creative products.
Exploratory processes concern their examination, interpretation, elaboration, and testing, including the search for useful functions or implications.
Exploration can reveal unexpected properties of an initially ambiguous structure and can lead back to further generation or modification.

Amabile's componential model likewise describes a creative process involving (a) problem or task identification, (b) preparation through gathering and reactivating relevant information and resources, (c) response generation through seeking and producing possible responses, and (d) response validation and communication through testing those responses against relevant criteria (Amabile, 1988 (Amabile, , 1996)).
text.formatted: Amabile's componential model likewise describes a creative process involving (a) problem or task identification, (b) preparation through gathering and reactivating relevant information and resources, (c) response generation through seeking and producing possible responses, and (d) response validation and communication through testing those responses against relevant criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Amabile, 1988</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amabile, , 1996))</ref>.

text.text: The resulting outcome can lead to completion or to further work on the task.
These activities operate within a broader framework of domain-relevant skills, creativity-relevant processes, task motivation, and the social environment.
Amabile's model therefore connects the development of an idea with the knowledge, motivation, and contextual conditions that support its generation and validation.
Despite their theoretical differences, these models contributed to a broader distinction between the generation of creative ideas and their subsequent evaluation and development.
This distinction is reflected in two-stage and three-stage descriptions of creativity.
However, these theories do not explicitly account for the different ways in which some creative ideas emerge into awareness.
Recent models offer a more detailed framework by emphasizing the interacting processes and systems involved in creative idea generation.

The dual pathway to creativity model proposed by Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel, and Baas distinguishes cognitive flexibility from cognitive persistence as contributors to creative ideation (Nijstad et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The dual pathway to creativity model proposed by Nijstad, De Dreu, Rietzschel, and Baas distinguishes cognitive flexibility from cognitive persistence as contributors to creative ideation <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Nijstad et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Flexibility supports movement between categories and perspectives, whereas persistence supports sustained exploration within a smaller set of possibilities.
Both can produce original and appropriate ideas.

Beaty and colleagues have integrated cognitive and neuroscientific findings to explain creative thought in terms of dynamic interactions among large-scale brain networks (Beaty et al., 2015 (Beaty et al., , 2016)).
text.formatted: Beaty and colleagues have integrated cognitive and neuroscientific findings to explain creative thought in terms of dynamic interactions among large-scale brain networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beaty et al., 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Beaty et al., , 2016))</ref>.

text.text: In particular, their work highlights cooperation between the default mode network, associated with internally generated thought, and executive control networks, which support the regulation of cognitive activity in relation to task goals and constraints.
Complementing this account, Benedek et al. (2016) distinguished the neural mechanisms associated with internally directed attention from those supporting selfgenerated thought.
text.formatted: Complementing this account, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Benedek et al. (2016)</ref> distinguished the neural mechanisms associated with internally directed attention from those supporting selfgenerated thought.

text.text: Together, these models highlight different dynamics of creative cognition, including cognitive flexibility and persistence, exploration and exploitation, and the interaction between spontaneous and controlled processes.
Nonetheless, how these cognitive processes lead to the emergence of an idea into conscious awareness remains unclear.
Other frameworks have focused more directly on the cognitive processes underlying illumination.

The explicit-implicit interaction (EII) theory of Hélie and Sun (2010), for example, explicitly describes "illumination" and proposes that interactions between explicit and implicit processing can explain how an idea becomes suddenly available to consciousness.
text.formatted: The explicit-implicit interaction (EII) theory of <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Hélie and Sun (2010)</ref>, for example, explicitly describes "illumination" and proposes that interactions between explicit and implicit processing can explain how an idea becomes suddenly available to consciousness.

text.text: Its implementation in the CLARION cognitive architecture provides a mechanistic framework of creative problem solving rather than simply another description of stages.

Re-examining Wallas's original model, Sadler-Smith (2015) argued that the familiar four-stage model does not fully capture Wallas's description of the creative process and restored intimation as a distinct stage between incubation and illumination.
text.formatted: Re-examining Wallas's original model, <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Sadler-Smith (2015)</ref> argued that the familiar four-stage model does not fully capture Wallas's description of the creative process and restored intimation as a distinct stage between incubation and illumination.

text.text: Intimation refers to a state of fringe consciousness in which an idea may be sensed as approaching before it becomes fully available, and Sadler-Smith situated incubation, intimation, and illumination along increasing levels of proximity to consciousness.
This account therefore provides an important precedent for distinguishing the processes preceding an idea from its eventual emergence into conscious awareness.
These contributions establish that the relationship between cognitive processing and conscious awareness has already been recognized as central to illumination.

What remains less systematically examined is the distinction between ideas that emerge suddenly into awareness, and those that develop gradually through a consciously accessible sequence of intermediate steps.
A further question concerns whether the way an idea emerges influences its quality.
Consider again the engineer's example introduced earlier.
One solution may take shape through the continuous modification of a design, whereas another may emerge after a sudden change in how the problem is represented.
Do these different ways of arriving at a solution produce equally good ideas?
Is one more likely to yield solutions that are original, useful, or correct?
And does the way an idea comes to mind influence how its creator evaluates it or makes subsequent decisions involving risk?

These questions are particularly consequential in design and engineering, where generating an idea is rarely sufficient: the resulting solution must ultimately satisfy practical constraints and, in many cases, work.
In sum, these contributions show that the correspondence between illumination and insight is not new, and that mechanisms underlying the sudden emergence of ideas have already been proposed.
Nevertheless, these theoretical connections have not been followed by a comparable integration of research on creative cognition and insight.

Research on creative cognition has predominantly investigated the generation, evaluation, and development of creative ideas, whereas insight research has accumulated extensive evidence concerning the processes that precede, accompany, and follow their sudden emergence into awareness.
The present chapter brings these two research traditions together to reconsider illumination within the broader process of creative idea generation.

Drawing on contemporary insight research, it examines the distinction between the gradual development of creative ideas and their sudden emergence into conscious awareness, and whether these different trajectories have consequences for the quality, evaluation, and subsequent development of creative ideas.
During the twentieth century, two major research traditions emerged to explain how novel ideas are generated.
One tradition developed within creativity research and focused on creative ideation, typically operationalized through divergent thinking (DT) tasks.

Originating from Guilford's theory (Guilford, 1967), this tradition emphasized the generation of multiple original ideas in response to open-ended problems, as operationalized, for example, in the Alternative Uses Task (AUT) and the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (Torrance, 1966).
text.formatted: Originating from Guilford's theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Guilford, 1967)</ref>, this tradition emphasized the generation of multiple original ideas in response to open-ended problems, as operationalized, for example, in the Alternative Uses Task (AUT) and the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">(Torrance, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: This framework focused on the cognitive processes supporting the generation and evaluation of multiple ideas, where creativity was conceptualized primarily in terms of fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration.
A second tradition developed within the problem-solving literature.

Introduced by the Gestalt school of psychology, insight research sought to explain how solutions can emerge through a sudden restructuring of the initial problem representation rather than through incremental, stepby-step search (Köhler, 1925; Maier, 1930;  for a review, see Vitello and Salvi, 2023).
text.formatted: Introduced by the Gestalt school of psychology, insight research sought to explain how solutions can emerge through a sudden restructuring of the initial problem representation rather than through incremental, stepby-step search <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Köhler, 1925;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Maier, 1930;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for a review, see <ref type="bibr">Vitello and Salvi, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, insight was not originally defined in terms of convergent thinking (CT).

Early research relied on classic insight problems, such as the nine-dot and candle problems (Duncker, 1945), because these problems were assumed to require a change in representation or the relaxation of implicit constraints.
text.formatted: Early research relied on classic insight problems, such as the nine-dot and candle problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Duncker, 1945)</ref>, because these problems were assumed to require a change in representation or the relaxation of implicit constraints.

text.text: Over time, however, insight research progressively shifted toward short, repeatable tasks with a single correct solution, including the Remote Associates Test (RAT), Compound Remote Associates (CRA) problems, anagrams, and rebus puzzles (Bowden et al., 2005; Bowden and Jung-Beeman, 2007; Salvi et al., 2016b Salvi et al., , 2020b)).
text.formatted: Over time, however, insight research progressively shifted toward short, repeatable tasks with a single correct solution, including the Remote Associates Test (RAT), Compound Remote Associates (CRA) problems, anagrams, and rebus puzzles <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bowden et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bowden and Jung-Beeman, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Salvi et al., 2016b</ref> <ref type="bibr">Salvi et al., , 2020b))</ref>.

text.text: This shift was primarily methodological rather than theoretical: these tasks provided many trials within a single experimental session, making it possible to distinguish insight from step-by-step solutions through self-reported Aha!
experiences and to combine behavioral measures with neurophysiological and neuroimaging methods.
The methodological choices made within the two traditions gradually produced what came to appear as a theoretical dichotomy.
Creativity researchers predominantly used open-ended DT tasks, whereas insight researchers predominantly used single-solution CT tasks.
Consequently, task structure became conflated with cognitive process: creative ideation became associated with DT, whereas insight became associated with CT.
Yet, neither association necessarily follows from the underlying cognitive processes.

DT and CT describe properties of the task and its solution space, particularly whether multiple possible responses or a single target solution are permitted, whereas insight concerns the cognitive processes and subjective experience through which a solution is reached.
The resulting DT-CT division therefore reinforced a methodological boundary between phenomena that may share important cognitive mechanisms.
As a consequence, creativity and insight research developed along parallel but largely non-interacting theoretical trajectories (Salvi et al., submitted).
text.formatted: As a consequence, creativity and insight research developed along parallel but largely non-interacting theoretical trajectories <ref type="bibr">(Salvi et al., submitted)</ref>.

text.text: This methodological separation may have exaggerated the differences between the two traditions while obscuring their shared cognitive foundations.
In particular, it may have discouraged researchers from examining whether the mechanisms traditionally investigated in insight problem solving also contribute to open-ended creative idea generation.

Both creative ideation and insight involve navigation of a semantic search space, retrieval and recombination of information from long-term memory, overcoming dominant associations, and the construction of representations that extend beyond immediately available information (Bowden and Jung Beeman, 1998; Jung-Beeman et al., 2004; Kenett et al., 2014; Kenett and Faust, 2019; Luchini et al., 2023; Madore et al., 2019; Mednick, 1962).
text.formatted: Both creative ideation and insight involve navigation of a semantic search space, retrieval and recombination of information from long-term memory, overcoming dominant associations, and the construction of representations that extend beyond immediately available information <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bowden and Jung Beeman, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Jung-Beeman et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Kenett et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Kenett and Faust, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Luchini et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Madore et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Mednick, 1962)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, several influential theorists anticipated this overlap decades ago. Guilford (1950) explicitly suggested that Gestalt notions of reorganization were relevant to creative thought, while Mednick's (1962) associative theory proposed a common mechanism whereby remote associations give rise to novel ideas, whether expressed in open-ended ideation or in problems with a single correct solution.
text.formatted: Indeed, several influential theorists anticipated this overlap decades ago. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Guilford (1950)</ref> explicitly suggested that Gestalt notions of reorganization were relevant to creative thought, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Mednick's (1962)</ref> associative theory proposed a common mechanism whereby remote associations give rise to novel ideas, whether expressed in open-ended ideation or in problems with a single correct solution.

text.text: Empirical evidence supports this convergence.

Behavioral, neurophysiological, and neuroimaging studies demonstrate substantial overlap between creative ideation and insight across memory retrieval, attentional regulation, cognitive control, semantic network organization, and affective-reward mechanisms (Salvi et al., submitted).
text.formatted: Behavioral, neurophysiological, and neuroimaging studies demonstrate substantial overlap between creative ideation and insight across memory retrieval, attentional regulation, cognitive control, semantic network organization, and affective-reward mechanisms <ref type="bibr">(Salvi et al., submitted)</ref>.

text.text: Despite these theoretical and empirical similarities, the methodological separation between creativity and insight research left a seemingly obvious question largely unexplored: can insight occur during DT?
Although there is no theoretical reason to restrict insight to problems with a single correct solution, experimental studies have begun to address this question only recently.
Research using generative tasks, including the AUT, has shown that Aha!
experiences occur during open-ended idea generation and that ideas accompanied by an Aha!
tend to receive higher creativity ratings than those generated without one (Moroshkina et al., 2026; Smith et al., 2026; McGuinness et al., 2026).
text.formatted: tend to receive higher creativity ratings than those generated without one <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Moroshkina et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Smith et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McGuinness et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These findings demonstrate that sudden, phenomenologically marked idea emergence is not restricted to convergent problem solving.
However, experiencing an Aha!
during DT does not indicate that insight has occurred.
Thus, before moving forward we need to distinguish several closely related concepts that have often been used interchangeably in the creativity and insight literatures.

According to a recent componential definition jointly developed by Salvi, Bhattacharya, and Ormerod (submitted to the Creativity Definitions Consensus project; Salvi et al., 2027), insight is defined as an event characterized by the sudden emergence of an idea, concept, or problem solution that is experienced as correct, novel, and effortless.
text.formatted: According to a recent componential definition jointly developed by Salvi, Bhattacharya, and Ormerod (submitted to the Creativity Definitions Consensus project; <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Salvi et al., 2027)</ref>, insight is defined as an event characterized by the sudden emergence of an idea, concept, or problem solution that is experienced as correct, novel, and effortless.

text.text: This is typically accompanied by a distinct shift in understanding and is often marked by an Aha!
experience.
The definition identifies three overlapping components: phenomenology, process, and product.
Phenomenology concerns the subjective experience of suddenness, surprise, pleasure, and clarity (summarized by the Aha!
experience).
Process refers to the cognitive mechanisms underlying insight, characterized by their relative opacity to introspection and nonlinear dynamics (e.g., nonlinear restructuring).
Product concerns the resulting idea or solution, particularly its correctness, novelty, and elegance.
The intersections between these components capture additional characteristics: the experience of effortlessness, the feeling of correctness, and the pragmatic fit of the resulting solution.
Their convergence characterizes true insight, whereas events involving only one or two components are classified as partial insights.
This distinction is particularly relevant to experimental research, where insight is frequently operationalized through self-reported Aha!
experiences.
Although the Aha!
experience captures important phenomenological characteristics of insight, it does not independently establish the cognitive processes underlying the solution.
Within this framework, illumination and insight are not synonymous.

Illumination refers to the sudden emergence of a creative idea into conscious awareness (consistent with its original position within Wallas's creative process (Wallas, 1926)) whereas insight encompasses the phenomenological, processing, and product-related characteristics described above.
text.formatted: Illumination refers to the sudden emergence of a creative idea into conscious awareness (consistent with its original position within Wallas's creative process <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Wallas, 1926)</ref>) whereas insight encompasses the phenomenological, processing, and product-related characteristics described above.

text.text: Insights can indeed occur outside the pure creative process, while illumination does not satisfy all the components of insight.

Restructuring, in turn, refers to a change in an existing representation of a problem or situation, a concept originating in the Gestalt tradition and subsequently formalized in cognitive theories of insight (Duncker, 1945; Knoblich et al., 1999; Ohlsson, 1984 Ohlsson, , 1992)).
text.formatted: Restructuring, in turn, refers to a change in an existing representation of a problem or situation, a concept originating in the Gestalt tradition and subsequently formalized in cognitive theories of insight <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Duncker, 1945;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Knoblich et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Ohlsson, 1984</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Ohlsson, , 1992))</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, restructuring can be understood as a meaningful change in how existing information is reorganized or reinterpreted.
While some scholars have argued that the restructuring and Aha!
experiences do not always correspond (Cushen and Wiley, 2012; Wiley and Danek, 2024) the two remain often conflated in experimental designs.

text.text: Many studies investigating insight in CT and DT tasks rely on self-reported Aha!
experiences without independently measuring restructuring and vice versa.
This distinction is particularly relevant to interpreting recent findings on Aha!
experiences during DT.

Understanding the cognitive processes operating within each creative stage is an important theoretical challenge in creativity research. Pinkow (2023), for example, argued that the creative process continues to contain a "black box," emphasizing the need to move beyond broad stage descriptions toward a more explicit specification of the underlying mechanisms.

text.text: To address this challenge, Figure 1: Dual-Route Model of Creative Idea Generation.
text.formatted: To address this challenge, Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>: Dual-Route Model of Creative Idea Generation.

text.text: Following preparation, creative ideas may emerge through two routes that differ in the conscious accessibility of intermediate processing.

Idea generation is followed by downstream processes, including evaluation, verification, elaboration, and implementation, which may lead to the selection or rejection of an idea or prompt a return to idea generation for further exploration and refinement.
the present framework draws on different theoretical approaches of problem solving.

Informationprocessing accounts describe problem solving as a search through intermediate states within a problem space (Newell and Simon, 1972), providing a foundation for understanding incremental, step-by-step solution processes.
text.formatted: Informationprocessing accounts describe problem solving as a search through intermediate states within a problem space <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Newell and Simon, 1972)</ref>, providing a foundation for understanding incremental, step-by-step solution processes.

text.text: Research on insight has further examined the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying different forms of problem solving, particularly those in which solutions emerge suddenly, with limited conscious access to the processing that precedes them (Kounios and Beeman, 2014; Metcalfe and Wiebe, 1987; Ohlsson, 1992).
text.formatted: Research on insight has further examined the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying different forms of problem solving, particularly those in which solutions emerge suddenly, with limited conscious access to the processing that precedes them <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Kounios and Beeman, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Metcalfe and Wiebe, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Ohlsson, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: The Dual-Route Model integrates these perspectives by specifying the cognitive organization of idea generation within the broader creative process, which includes preparation, idea generation, and the downstream processes through which ideas are evaluated, selected, refined, or rejected.
Preparation involves the cognitive and attentional states that may influence subsequent idea generation, including those established before the problem is encountered.
The model proposes that ideas can emerge through two routes.
The continuous route involves step-by-step exploration in which intermediate processing remains relatively accessible to conscious awareness.

The discontinuous route, which encompasses incubation and illumination, involves critical intermediate processing that remains comparatively inaccessible until an idea suddenly becomes consciously available.
Ideas emerging through either route may subsequently undergo evaluation, verification, elaboration, and further development, potentially leading to implementation or rejection ( see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Ideas emerging through either route may subsequently undergo evaluation, verification, elaboration, and further development, potentially leading to implementation or rejection ( see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: These downstream processes may feed back into idea generation when a candidate is rejected or modified, or when it prompts further search.

The model does not posit two separate idea-generating systems analogous to those proposed in classical dual-process accounts, nor does it map the two routes onto different classes of creativity tasks.
Continuous and discontinuous processing instead describe alternative trajectories through which individual candidate ideas may develop and become available to awareness.

Accordingly, CT and DT can recruit either route: a convergent problem may be solved through step-by-step analysis or insight, while individual ideas generated during DT may likewise develop through relatively continuous processing or emerge discontinuously.
The EII theory provides an important mechanistic precedent for this account through its implemen-tation within the CLARION cognitive architecture (Hélie and Sun, 2010).
text.formatted: The EII theory provides an important mechanistic precedent for this account through its implemen-tation within the CLARION cognitive architecture <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hélie and Sun, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: EII connects Wallas's stages with interacting explicit and implicit processes.
Explicit knowledge is represented through identifiable concepts and rules, whereas implicit knowledge relies on distributed representations supporting associative processing.
Both forms of processing can operate simultaneously, and their outputs can be integrated across successive rounds of processing.
Within EII, preparation and verification rely more heavily on explicit processing, whereas incubation places greater weight on implicit processing.
A candidate becomes reportable when an internal confidence measure crosses a threshold, and a large, sudden increase following integration can correspond to an intense Aha!
experience (Hélie and Sun, 2010).
text.formatted: experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hélie and Sun, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The computational model reproduced selected findings concerning incubation, recall, and insight problem solving, providing a concrete example of how ongoing processing can culminate in a sudden conscious outcome without implying that this implementation is the only possible mechanism.
The Dual-Route Model builds on this precedent but makes a different distinction.

The explicit and implicit levels of CLARION should not be mapped one-to-one onto the continuous and discontinuous routes, because both routes may involve interactions between explicit and implicit processing.
Instead, the present framework distinguishes routes according to how their products become available to awareness, separating this temporal distinction from the mechanisms that may produce them.
In this respect, it also differs from the flexibility-persistence pathways proposed by Nijstad et al. (2010).
text.formatted: In this respect, it also differs from the flexibility-persistence pathways proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Nijstad et al. (2010)</ref>.

text.text: Flexible exploration and persistent search describe different ways of navigating an idea space, either of which may contribute to continuous development or culminate in a discontinuous transition.
The two routes are therefore not proposed as independent cognitive systems, but as alternative processing dynamics within idea generation.
The continuous route is characterized by intermediate states that remain relatively accessible to awareness, allowing the individual to monitor and guide the development of an idea.
Candidate ideas or solutions can be compared with the current representation, revised in light of new information, and further elaborated as search unfolds.
Continuity here does not imply that a fully formed idea enters consciousness gradually.
Rather, continuity refers to the accessibility of the generative trajectory.

Early metacognitive studies provided some of the first empirical evidence for differences in the accessibility of intermediate solution states. Metcalfe (1986a) found that prospective feelings of knowing were poor predictors of subsequent solutions to insight problems, suggesting that people have limited awareness of their progress toward a solution.
text.formatted: Early metacognitive studies provided some of the first empirical evidence for differences in the accessibility of intermediate solution states. <ref type="bibr">Metcalfe (1986a)</ref> found that prospective feelings of knowing were poor predictors of subsequent solutions to insight problems, suggesting that people have limited awareness of their progress toward a solution.

text.text: Subsequently, Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) examined feelings of warmth, or the subjective sense of approaching a solution, during problem solving.
text.formatted: Subsequently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987)</ref> examined feelings of warmth, or the subjective sense of approaching a solution, during problem solving.

text.text: For noninsight problems, warmth ratings increased progressively as participants approached a solution, whereas insight problems were characterized by relatively stable ratings followed by an abrupt increase near solution.

These findings provided an early metacognitive basis for distinguishing continuous problem solving, in which progress can be monitored through intermediate states, from solutions that emerge with little anticipation.

Further evidence concerning the cognitive processes supporting step-by-step solving comes from studies examining working memory and cognitive load. Fleck (2008) found that working-memory capacity is associated with performance on step-by-step problems, whereas verbal short-term-memory capacity is more closely associated with insight problem solving.
text.formatted: Further evidence concerning the cognitive processes supporting step-by-step solving comes from studies examining working memory and cognitive load. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fleck (2008)</ref> found that working-memory capacity is associated with performance on step-by-step problems, whereas verbal short-term-memory capacity is more closely associated with insight problem solving.

text.text: These findings suggest that maintaining and manipulating information contributes to step-by-step solution development.

More direct evidence comes from Stuyck et al. (2022), who manipulated cognitive load during problem solving and found that increasing load made step-by-step solutions slower and less frequent, whereas insight solutions were comparatively unaffected.
text.formatted: More direct evidence comes from <ref type="bibr">Stuyck et al. (2022)</ref>, who manipulated cognitive load during problem solving and found that increasing load made step-by-step solutions slower and less frequent, whereas insight solutions were comparatively unaffected.

text.text: This pattern suggests that step-by-step solving depends more strongly on capacity-limited cognitive resources, consistent with the maintenance and monitoring of intermediate solution states.
Importantly, step-by-step solving should not be understood as a single, uniform strategy.
Using verbal protocols, Fleck and Weisberg (2013) documented different approaches to problem solving, including the application of existing knowledge and heuristic search.
text.formatted: Using verbal protocols, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Fleck and Weisberg (2013)</ref> documented different approaches to problem solving, including the application of existing knowledge and heuristic search.

text.text: Their findings highlight the diversity of processes through which solutions can be developed progressively.

Within the present framework, these studies complement the metacognitive evidence by suggesting that the continuous route involves intermediate states that can be monitored and used to guide subsequent processing, supported by working-memory resources.
However, the involvement of working memory or cognitive control does not establish that every underlying operation is always consciously accessible.
Rather, the defining feature of the continuous route is the relative accessibility of intermediate states as an idea develops.
People may deliberately explore possibilities, evaluate alternatives, and progressively develop an idea through conscious thought, while other processes potentially contribute outside awareness.
The unconscious analytic thought account proposed by Macchi et al. (2019) suggests that systematic, goal-directed processing may occur without conscious access.
text.formatted: The unconscious analytic thought account proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Macchi et al. (2019)</ref> suggests that systematic, goal-directed processing may occur without conscious access.

text.text: More recently, Macchi et al. (2026) found sustained pupil dilation during incubation among participants who subsequently solved an insight problem, consistent with continued cognitive effort despite the suspension of deliberate problem solving.
text.formatted: More recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Macchi et al. (2026)</ref> found sustained pupil dilation during incubation among participants who subsequently solved an insight problem, consistent with continued cognitive effort despite the suspension of deliberate problem solving.

text.text: Although these findings concern insight rather than continuous idea generation, they raise the possibility that consciously accessible, step-by-step development may coexist with processing that remains outside awareness.

People may not consciously select one route in advance; instead, idea generation may begin through accessible, step-by-step processing, while the relative contributions of accessible and inaccessible processing change throughout the generative episode.
Thus, whether and how processing outside awareness contributes to the continuous route remains an important question for future research.

The discontinuous route is characterized by limited conscious access to intermediate states, such that an individual may move from having no consciously available candidate idea to its sudden emergence into awareness.
Importantly, this discontinuity concerns conscious access rather than necessarily the underlying cognitive processes, which may unfold over time without being accessible as a progressive sequence.
Illumination refers to this sudden emergence of a creative idea into awareness, which is regularly accompanied by an Aha!
experience, especially when the emerging idea involves a meaningful change in the individual's existing mental representation.
Early evidence consistent with this distinction comes from Metcalfe (1986b), whose investigation revealed that feelings of knowing did not reliably predict subsequent success on insight problems.

Together, these metacognitive findings support the view that, during discontinuous problem solving, solution-relevant information becomes consciously available in an all-or-none manner.

Several studies have shown that incubation can facilitate subsequent problem solving and creative idea generation.
For example, Baird et al. (2012) found that performance on previously encountered DT problems improved following an incubation period involving an undemanding task.

text.text: An alternative explanation is provided by the forgetting-fixation hypothesis, which proposes that initial attempts to solve a problem can strengthen unproductive associations or interpretations, making alternative solutions more difficult to access.
Temporarily setting the problem aside allows these dominant but unhelpful responses to become less accessible, reducing their interference with subsequent problem solving.
When the individual returns to the task, previously overlooked alternatives may therefore become easier to retrieve or explore.

Incubation is therefore best understood as a condition that can facilitate subsequent creative performance through different processes, rather than as evidence for a single form of unconscious problem solving.
Importantly, putting a problem a side is different from an interruption of deliberate work, and the first may not be necessary for discontinuous idea emergence.

However, their underlying cognitive dynamics remain unknown, and should not be equated with incubation as traditionally defined (i.e., putting a side a problem).
Whether processing during such pauses shares mechanisms with experimentally induced incubation is an empirical question that future studies need to adress.
Within the Dual-Route Model, incubation is therefore considered a possible context for the processes preceding illumination, rather than a necessary stage of the discontinuous route.
Maintaining this distinction is important because equating incubation with any unobserved processing before an idea would make the concept difficult to operationalize and test.
Experimentally defined incubation involves a period of disengagement from the target task, whereas the processing preceding sudden idea emergence may also occur during ongoing exploration.
Whether these circumstances engage similar mechanisms, and whether they involve representational restructuring, requires further empirical investigation.
Illumination An idea may result from extended processing while its emergence into awareness is experienced as sudden.

This distinction is particularly relevant to illumination, a term that retains something of its original metaphorical meaning: bringing into the "light" of awareness an idea whose preceding development was largely hidden from introspection.
Understanding illumination therefore requires examining how information contributing to an idea may develop before the idea itself becomes consciously available.

Research on insight problem solving provides relevant evidence for this distinction, showing that solution-related information can become activated before individuals are able to identify or report a solution.
In the classic accumulation-of-clues paradigm, Bowers et al. (1990) found that participants progressively accumulated information relevant to a solution before they could explicitly identify it.

text.text: Insight occurs when the accumulated evidence makes it possible to abandon less useful interpretations and reorganize the problem around a better one.
Although processing develops over time, the resulting emergence into awareness can be abrupt and feel sudden.
This model illustrates how gradual information accumulation can culminate in a discontinuous change in understanding, providing a possible mechanism for the sudden emergence of an idea.

In addition, pupillometry provides a complementary approach to examining physiological changes surrounding moments in which a previously unavailable interpretation or solution becomes consciously accessible.
A useful parallel comes from bistable perception.

When viewing an ambiguous figure such as the Necker cube, the physical stimulus remains unchanged while its interpretation suddenly switches from one percept to another. Einhäuser et al. text.text: The journey of an idea is as important as its destination.
But are ideas that emerge suddenly any more creative than those developed through a gradual, step-by-step process?

Historically, this question has been addressed almost exclusively within convergent problem solving, where quality can be evaluated against an objective criterion: a proposed solution is either correct or incorrect.

Across this literature, a remarkably consistent pattern has emerged: insight is associated with successful problem solving, both when examined in terms of representational restructuring, which can facilitate reaching correct solutions (Knoblich et al., 1999; Kershaw and Ohlsson, 2004; Öllinger et al., 2008), and when assessed through measuring the Aha!

This finding is relevant to the distinction between the two routes proposed here.
In the continuous route, intermediate products remain relatively accessible as the candidate idea develops and can be monitored, evaluated, and revised.

In the discontinuous route the idea becomes available more abruptly, with comparatively limited access to the intermediate products preceding it (Metcalfe and Wiebe, 1987; Smith and Kounios, 1996; Kounios and Beeman, 2014; Salvi, 2023).

text.text: The Aha!
experience should therefore be understood as an informative metacognitive cue rather than a guarantee of correctness.
Crucially, however, the evidence establishing the insight-accuracy relationship has been obtained almost entirely in convergent problem-solving contexts.
As mentioned in the former section, this reflects the historical and methodological development of the field rather than a theoretical reason to restrict insight to convergent cognition.
Consequently, for much of the history of insight research, asking whether insight produced a "better" idea effectively meant asking whether it produced a more accurate solution.
Extending the study of insight to DT changes the relevant criterion of quality.
In an AUT, for example, there is no solution key against which an idea can be classified as correct or incorrect.
Instead, successful ideas are those that depart from common or readily accessible responses while remaining appropriate to the task, and they can be classified as more or less original or elaborated.

If the relationship observed in convergent problem solving reflects something more general about the quality of cognitive products that emerge through insight, its behavioral expression should therefore change with the structure of the task.
In CT, having an insight increases the probability of reaching the correct solution; in DT, the corresponding advantage may instead be expressed as increased creativity.

While in CT Aha!
intensity was strongly associated with objective accuracy (consistent with the insight-accuracy effect), in DT the relationship between Aha!
and creative quality was more modest, whereas the relationship with participants' own judgments of creativity was considerably stronger.
The authors termed this discrepancy the "Aha!
glow": experiencing an Aha!
can make an idea feel particularly creative even when the corresponding advantage in externally evaluated creativity is smaller.
Thus, while the Aha!
experience appears to provide a relatively well-calibrated cue to correctness in constrained problem solving, its relation to quality becomes more complex when the criterion itself is open-ended.
Taken together, these findings suggest a potentially important parallel between CT and DT, but not a simple equivalence between accuracy and creativity.
In CT tasks, insight distinguishes candidate solutions that are likely to satisfy an externally specified criterion: the correct solution.

In DT tasks, the emerging evidence indicates that Aha!-accompanied ideas can also be more original or creative, while simultaneously showing that the subjective experience of insight may amplify creators' evaluations of their own ideas.
Two complementary explanations may account for the relationship between Aha!
experiences and creative quality.

First, the processing preceding sudden idea emergence may facilitate access to more remote associations or alternative representations, producing ideas that are more original at the moment they become available.
Second, the Aha!
experience may influence subsequent processing by increasing attention to an emerging idea and motivating its elaboration.
On this account, part of the creative advantage associated with Aha!
could arise from the downstream effects that follow the experience.
The first explanation concerns the processes that generate an idea; the second concerns what happens after the idea has emerged.
Distinguishing these possibilities will require separating the quality of an idea from the effects of subsequent elaboration and evaluation.
Restructuring provides one possible mechanism for this relationship, but it remains to be demonstrated directly in DT.
The available evidence primarily concerns ideas accompanied by an Aha!
experience rather than independently identified continuous and discontinuous routes.

Whether the advantages associated with insight reflect the underlying trajectory of idea generation, representational restructuring, or the subsequent effects of insight phenomenology remains to be established.

This distinction is particularly relevant to the present model, because the route through which an idea emerges and the processes that determine its subsequent fate may interact without being identical.
Once an idea becomes available to awareness, it is evaluated and may then be developed and potentially translated into action.
In other words, once we have an idea, what do we do with it?
More importantly, does the manner in which an idea is generated influence what happens to it next?
This question extends the Dual-Route Model beyond idea generation to the consequences of how ideas emerge into awareness.
A relatively small body of research on the downstream effects of insight provides an initial basis for addressing it.
Early evidence comes from Salvi and Bowden (2019), who showed that problem-solving accuracy and confidence are related to subsequent judgments and decisions.

text.text: influences subsequent decision-making.
After solving verbal problems, participants chose between a certain monetary reward and an uncertain reward offering a potentially higher payoff.
Choices of the uncertain option were more frequent following solutions accompanied by an Aha!
experience than those without one, suggesting that the Aha!
experience may temporarily increase risk preference.

Extending these findings, Becker et al. (2023) replicated the behavioral effect and found greater activation in the nucleus accumbens, a region implicated in reward processing, following high-compared with low-Aha!

text.text: experiences.
Thus, the rewarding phenomenology of insight may have motivational consequences extending beyond the problem that elicited it.
This finding has important implications for creative practice because pursuing an idea often involves uncertainty, particularly in DT, where there may be no immediately verifiable correct solution.
Here, the Aha!
experience may encourage individuals to pursue an idea whose value is not yet known, potentially promoting exploration of unconventional possibilities that might otherwise be dismissed.
However, the same mechanism could also increase commitment to an idea simply because its emergence felt compelling.
To date, there is little evidence establishing how Aha!
experiences influence subsequent risk-taking, idea selection, or willingness to invest in ideas generated during DT.
This represents both a potential adaptive function and a potential vulnerability of the Aha!
experience: increased willingness to pursue unexpected ideas may facilitate creative exploration, but it may also encourage investment in ideas whose value has not yet been established.
In this sense, the Aha!

experience resembles Alice's decision to follow the White Rabbit into Wonderland: an unexpected discovery may open possibilities that would otherwise remain unexplored, but the initial sense of curiosity and excitement offers no guarantee that the path will lead somewhere worthwhile!
Beyond their influence on decision-making, Aha!
experiences also have consequences for memory, a relationship supported by a substantial body of empirical evidence.
Several studies have demonstrated that problem solutions associated with an Aha!
moment tend to be better remembered (i.e., the so-called insight memory advantage).
Specifically, Danek et al. (2013) demonstrated that these solutions were better recalled two weeks later than solutions reached without that experience.

Kizilirmak and colleagues (2016) found that both spontaneous and induced insights were associated with better subsequent memory.

Importantly, both representational change and hippocampal activity were associated with better subsequent memory for correctly identified objects, even when accounting for solution time.

experiences was better remembered than information encountered when these feelings were missing.
The consequences of insight may therefore extend beyond retaining a newly generated idea to facilitating learning from information encountered around the same time.
How can we explain these effects?
One explanation concerns the rewarding experience accompanying insight.
The sudden change in understanding characteristic of insight is often accompanied by positive affect, confidence, and a sense that the new interpretation is meaningful.
These features may engage reward-related processes that contribute to the encoding and retention of newly acquired information.
A computational account proposed by Laukkonen et al. (2023) offers a framework for understanding this relationship.
text.formatted: A computational account proposed by <ref type="bibr">Laukkonen et al. (2023)</ref> offers a framework for understanding this relationship.

text.text: According to this account, representational restructuring generates a higher-order prediction error, while dopaminergic precision-weighting contributes to the confidence, pleasure, and motivational salience associated with the Aha!
experience.
The resulting combination of representational change and reward-related signaling may help explain why information acquired through insight is particularly memorable.
Within the Dual-Route Model, these findings suggest that the consequences of idea generation may depend on both the processes that produce an idea and the experience accompanying its emergence.

As illustrated in Figure 1, a consciously available candidate may subsequently undergo evaluation, verification, elaboration, selection, or implementation, depending on the individual's goals and the demands of the task.

text.text: These processes are conditional rather than necessary stages.
The Aha!
experience may influence which ideas receive further attention, how willing individuals are to pursue them, and what information is retained for later use.
The convergence between attention, decision-making, and memory raises a broader question.
Why should a sudden change in understanding simultaneously feel rewarding, command attention, promote action, and facilitate learning?
One possibility is that these effects are different expressions of an adaptive mechanism for updating internal models.
If insight marks a consequential change in representation, its characteristic phenomenology may help prioritize and stabilize that change so that it can influence future cognition and behavior.
While the Dual-Route Model proposed in this chapter aims to explain how ideas emerge during creative cognition, the processes associated with insight may serve a broader function beyond creativity.
For example, sudden changes in understanding have been described across problem solving, perception, psychotherapy, social understanding, and meditation (Ke et al., 2026; Tulver et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, sudden changes in understanding have been described across problem solving, perception, psychotherapy, social understanding, and meditation <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Ke et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Tulver et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Across these contexts, having an insight reflects a more general capacity to reorganize available information, allowing a new interpretation to revise an existing one.
This raises the possibility that insight may serves a broader adaptive function: updating the internal models through which our mind interprets information available in the world.
Predictive-processing accounts provide a potential theoretical framework for this interpretation.
Cognition can be conceived as relying on generative models that organize incoming information and generate predictions about the world (Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: Cognition can be conceived as relying on generative models that organize incoming information and generate predictions about the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: When incoming information can no longer be accommodated by an existing model, prediction errors create pressure for updating.

Such updating can occur gradually, as accumulating evidence progressively modifies the existing model, or via insight (Laukkonen et al., 2023). Friston et al. (2017) relate insight to Bayesian model reduction, whereby a more parsimonious model can emerge through the removal of redundant or poorly supported parameters.

(2017)</ref> relate insight to Bayesian model reduction, whereby a more parsimonious model can emerge through the removal of redundant or poorly supported parameters.

text.text: Building on this framework, Laukkonen et al. (2023) propose that restructuring through Bayesian reduction generates a higher-order prediction error associated with the content of insight.

text.text: Dopaminergic precision-weighting of this prediction error is proposed to contribute to the confidence, pleasure, and attentional capture characteristic of the Aha!
experience.
Recent computational work provides a proof of principle for this possibility.

Using an active-inference model, Doulfoukar et al. (2026) demonstrated how gradual evidence accumulation can precede an abrupt reorganization of an internal model through Bayesian model reduction, accompanied by discontinuous changes in behavior and confidence, a transient increase in Bayesian surprise, and increased expected precision.

text.text: In sum, restructuring concerns the change in the representation, whereas the Aha!
experience may signal the significance of that change to the cognitive system.
This perspective offers a potential explanation for the convergence of findings considered in the preceding sections.

If insight marks a consequential change in representation, the positive affect, confidence, and motivational salience accompanying its emergence may help prioritize the new interpretation, while reward-related neuromodulatory processes may create conditions favorable to its consolidation.
The relationship between insight and memory is particularly relevant here.
When restructuring produces a more adequate representation, retaining that update may improve the individual's ability to interpret subsequent information and guide future behavior.
The memory advantage associated with insight may therefore reflect, at least in part, mechanisms that favor the stabilization of newly reorganized representations.

As a consequence, insight might transiently promote plasticity around a successful model update, strengthening the newly reorganized representation and facilitating learning from information encountered around the same time.
While this proposal could account for the convergence among insight, reward, memory, and learning, it remains (so far) a hypothesis.
Whether insight itself produces a transient increase in neural plasticity, and whether dopaminergic mechanisms causally mediate such an effect, has yet to be experimentally established.
Importantly, this possibility also raises the question of whether the Aha!
experience contributes to the stabilization of a new representation independently of the restructuring that produced it.

Distinguishing the effects of representational change from those of its accompanying phenomenology would help clarify whether the memory advantage reflects successful model updating, the rewarding experience of insight, or their interaction.
This perspective also clarifies why insight is useful without being infallible.
If the Aha!
experience evolved or developed as a probabilistic signal of successful model revision, it need not perfectly discriminate correct from incorrect representations.
When the signal tracks a genuine improvement in the model, prioritizing and retaining the new interpretation is adaptive.
When the same phenomenology accompanies an erroneous restructuring, however, confidence, reward, and enhanced retention could instead stabilize a false interpretation.

The mechanisms that allow insight to rapidly revise an inadequate model may therefore also help explain why false insights can become unusually compelling and resistant to revision (Laukkonen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The mechanisms that allow insight to rapidly revise an inadequate model may therefore also help explain why false insights can become unusually compelling and resistant to revision <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Laukkonen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Evaluation and verification remain critical precisely because the subjective strength of the update cannot guarantee its objective validity.
This broader interpretation is also relevant to creative cognition.

The discontinuous route may contribute to the generation of new ideas by allowing previously dominant organizations of a problem or semantic space to be escaped, permitting information to be recombined or interpreted from a different perspective.
When this transition involves genuine restructuring, the resulting Aha!
experience may help the new idea capture attention and remain available for further development.
In open-ended creative thinking, therefore, the potential adaptive function of Aha!
may lie in marking a candidate representation as worth exploring.
Its eventual value must be established downstream through evaluation, elaboration, testing, and, where appropriate, verification.
This returns us to the architecture of the Dual-Route Model.
The continuous and discontinuous routes describe how candidate ideas develop and become available to awareness; they do not themselves determine what happens afterward.

Illumination marks the sudden emergence of an idea through the discontinuous route, while insight refers to the more specific case in which that emergence reflects a change in representation and is accompanied by an Aha!
experience.
Once available, the candidate enters a different problem: whether it should be retained, elaborated, tested, implemented, or rejected.
The phenomenology of insight may bias this downstream competition by attracting attention, encouraging exploration, and strengthening retention, but it does not replace evaluation.
The route by which an idea reaches awareness and the fate of that idea after it arrives are therefore distinct, but potentially interacting, components of creative cognition.

The deeper question is whether the cognitive machinery underlying insight evolved more generally to enable consequential and stable changes in how an organism understands, remembers, and acts upon its world.
The most immediate test of the Dual-Route Model is whether the processing dynamics identified for insight in convergent problem solving generalize to DT.

Much of the evidence reviewed in this chapter for discontinuous processing comes from CT tasks: insight solutions are characterized by limited access to intermediate states, abrupt changes in perceived proximity to solution, distinctive attentional and physiological dynamics, and, under some conditions, representational restructuring.
Recent studies demonstrate that Aha!
experiences also occur during DT and are associated with more creative ideas (Smith et al., 2026; Moroshkina et al., 2026; McGuinness et al., 2026), but the presence of an Aha!

text.text: experience alone does not establish that the same underlying processes are involved.
The critical next step is therefore to examine the trajectory surrounding individual Aha!-associated ideas in open-ended problems.
This will require testing whether the behavioral, metacognitive, and neurocognitive markers established in CT can also identify discontinuous emergence during DT.

These markers should be examined at the level of individual ideas, using converging measures of perceived progress, response timing, gaze and attentional dynamics, pupil responses, neural activity, and changes in search trajectory.

The critical prediction concerns access to the generative trajectory: during continuous processing, intermediate states should remain sufficiently accessible to be monitored and manipulated, whereas before discontinuous emergence, critical intermediate states should remain comparatively inaccessible until their product becomes consciously available.
Importantly, the model does not predict that the processes preceding discontinuous emergence are themselves instantaneous.

Substantial processing may unfold over time before culminating in an abrupt transition into awareness, as suggested by both the empirical evidence reviewed here and recent computational modeling (Doulfoukar et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Substantial processing may unfold over time before culminating in an abrupt transition into awareness, as suggested by both the empirical evidence reviewed here and recent computational modeling <ref type="bibr">(Doulfoukar et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The question goes beyond demonstrating that Aha!
experiences occur during DT, to demonstrating if the two routes are (for example) accompanied by the same physiological markers of discontinuous processing observed in CT.
A second challenge is to establish restructuring in DT.
Aha!

experiences during DT show that sudden, phenomenologically salient idea emergence is not confined to CT problems (Smith et al., 2026; Moroshkina et al., 2026), but they do not demonstrate that restructuring has occurred.

text.text: Future studies should therefore seek independent evidence of representational change, for example through changes in the organization of successive responses, semantic search trajectories, or experimental manipulations of the representation through which a problem is approached.
This distinction is essential for determining when illumination occurs within DT.
It is equally important for testing whether restructuring itself predicts the quality of an idea, or whether some of the advantages associated with insight arise just from the Aha!
experience and its downstream effects.
A third question concerns what happens after an idea becomes consciously available.

Evaluation and verification should not be assumed to follow every instance of idea generation, but may depend on epistemic motivation, task demands, external incentives, anticipated consequences, and the need to act.
Future work should examine whether the route through which an idea emerges influences its subsequent fate: whether it is remembered, selected, elaborated, tested, implemented, or rejected.
This question may be particularly important in open-ended creative and design contexts, where an Aha!
experience can make an idea feel compelling in the absence of an immediately available criterion of correctness.
The emerging evidence on memory, confidence, and risk preference therefore generates a testable prediction: ideas accompanied by stronger Aha!
experiences may receive preferential attention and investment even when their objective quality is held constant.

Establishing when this prioritization is adaptive, and when it instead contributes to premature commitment to a compelling but inadequate idea, is an important direction for future research and practical applications.
A particularly important question concerns the developmental origins of the two routes.
The distinction between continuous and discontinuous processing does not imply that they emerge simultaneously in ontogeny.

Predictive processing is evident early in infancy: six-month-olds show pupillary responses to violations of learned predictions (Zhang et al., 2019), and nine-month-olds show enhanced theta activity to unexpected physical and social events, consistent with early predictionerror processing (Köster et al., 2021).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that mechanisms for detecting discrepancies between predictions and incoming information, and for using such discrepancies to guide subsequent learning and information seeking, are present well before mature executive and metacognitive abilities.
The developmental literature on insight similarly suggests that some components of discontinuous processing are present relatively early.
Aha!

experiences have been reported in young children, and their frequency appears relatively stable between four and eight years even as children's understanding of what those experiences represent becomes more sophisticated (Prenevost et al., 2025).

text.text: Thus, the capacity for discontinuous emergence may precede the capacity to understand or report the metacognitive significance of that transition.
These results raise the question of whether continuous and discontinuous processing follow different developmental trajectories.

Mature continuous processing requires sustained access to intermediate states that can be monitored, evaluated, and deliberately manipulated, whereas discontinuous emergence does not necessarily require conscious access to the computations producing its product.
Discontinuous processing could reflect an earlier-developing form of cognition that is progressively complemented by greater conscious access to generative processing.
Alternatively, both processing dynamics may be present early and become increasingly differentiated and strategically regulated over development.

Distinguishing these possibilities would help establish whether developmental changes occur primarily in the mechanisms that generate new representations, in access to those processes, or in the metacognitive ability to recognize and evaluate their products.
Testing these hypotheses will require measures that do not depend exclusively on verbal reports of insight.
Pupillometry provides one promising approach because it can be applied across developmental stages.
In adults, pupil dilation has been observed shortly before solutions reported as insight (Salvi et al., 2020c).
